editorial.headline: Everyday Footwear Manufacturing, Open Across Scales
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the making of daily-use footwear and its component parts, with national PMA openness and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
**This activity is the industrial making of footwear for ordinary daily use.** The record describes shoes and sandals made from leather and imitation leather, rubber, textiles, plastic, and wood: daily shoes, casual shoes, sandal-shoes, wooden sandals, slippers, and similar products. It also reaches into the manufacture of the parts that make those products usable and finished: uppers, insoles, outer soles, front, middle, and rear reinforcements, linings, and accessories made from the same stated materials.

That scope matters because this is not framed as a narrow retail activity or a design-only business. It is manufacturing. A founder reading the category should see a production activity: cutting, forming, assembling, finishing, or otherwise making the footwear or the listed components that belong to it. The record is broad in materials and practical in product type, but it remains anchored to everyday footwear rather than specialised or ceremonial use. Its commercial centre is the ordinary object people wear daily, produced at industrial or workshop scale depending on the registered business size.

The scale position is clean. The record marks the activity as open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. In practical registration language, that means the slim record does not reserve the activity to one size band; it can sit with very small operators, small and medium businesses, or larger manufacturing companies. The national PMA position is also straightforward: the activity is marked TERBUKA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. There is no basis in the record to invent an additional national condition, capital threshold, licence timeline, or special manufacturing test. The available fact is simply that, nationally, foreign ownership is open up to the stated ceiling.

Bali is not presented as a hidden obstacle here. The moratorium rule in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA across the province, but this activity is not marked as blocked. The record gives its Bali status as OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, with the reason stated as: OSS risk at scale Besar is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi → not blocked by moratorium. The honest reading is therefore balanced but clear: nationally, it is open to PMA up to 100%; in Bali, the record does not mark it as blocked by the moratorium. For this activity, the national openness and the Bali-side status point in the same direction rather than pulling founders into a contradiction.
